newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's showman president takes bow to austerity.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's showman president takes bow to austerity.

text.p: Abdala Bucaram, who campaigned as a champion of the poor, rode to the ornate presidential palace in Quito on a wave of popular discontent with Ecuador's discredited political establishment.
But just six months later a tidal backwash sent him reeling back into private life in one of the quickest downfalls in the turbulent history of Latin American heads of state.

Bucaram, a burly man of Lebanese descent with a pockmarked face and bald pate, portrayed himself as a working-class hero as he steamrolled across Ecuador on the campaign trail -- rallying the poor with fiery anti-establishment speeches.

He was an especially harsh critic of multilateral lending agencies and what he described as their open meddling in the affairs of sovereign states. "The poor have always had a secret love, and that is Abdala Bucaram," he said in one interview shortly before his election in July 1996.

But organised labour and political opposition groups started suspecting he was little more than "a neo-liberal in populist clothing" after he sought out the advice of former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo to help devise an economic plan based on austerity and fiscal discipline.

Cavallo, a prestigious but highly controversial figure in his homeland, was credited with reining in Argentina's runaway inflation. But the advice he dished out to Bucaram undoubtedly took a political toll, just as calls for economic belt-tightening helped erode support for Brazil's Fernando Collor de Mello and Venezuela's Carlos Andres Perez -- the other South American presidents ousted this decade.

Much was said about the eccentric behaviour and public antics of the man popularly known as "El Loco" since he took office. Memorable moments included his rock 'n' roll stage acts and luncheon with Lorena Bobbit -- the Ecuador-born American who had sliced off her husband's penis.

But Bucaram was declared mentally incompetent and voted out of office by Congress on Thursday, after a massive nationwide strike shut down most of Ecuador in protest against the harsh economic austerity measures his government unveiled in December and early January.

Those measures were something investment bankers and World Bank economists no doubt heralded with glee. But they marked a blow to Ecuador's vast majority of poor. The measures included electricity and gas rate hikes totalling more than 200 percent and a 60 percent rise in bus fares. Telephone rates jumped a full 600 percent.
"That (the price hikes) was definitely what turned the people against him," said Santiago Nieto, an analyst with Informe Confidencial, Ecuador's leading financial weekly.
"It was a real shot in the foot," added a Western diplomat. "The austerity measures left Bucaram limping."

Reports of rampant government corruption and nepotism, and of Bucaram's alleged free-spending ways, did little to bolster his image with minimum wage earners taking home less than $100 a month. He recently assumed the presidency of the Barcelona soccer team in Guayaquil, for instance, and word that he had agreed to pay Diego Maradona -- the former Argentine soccer star -- $1 million to play a single match with the team struck raw nerves in Ecuador.

The embattled Bucaram visited a working-class district on the outskirts of his native Guayaquil on Saturday, in an apparent bid to test which way the political winds were blowing in his old powerbase.
The crowd looked small and unenthusiastic and Bucaram got little more than a bemused look from most onlookers when he described himself as "the commander-in-chief of the poor."
Hours later, in a pre-dawn interview on national television, he conceded for the first time since the no-confidence vote against him on Thursday that he had lost any futher ability to rule.
